[[RunningHead]]

Psychoanalysis—For an Elite?

Rose Spiegel M.D.

Rose Spiegel

Rose Spiegel, M.D.
350 Central Park West
New York, N.Y. 10025

Rose Spiegel  

MANY ATTACKS and criticisms have been levelled at psychoanalysis, some of them mutually contradictory: It is a "religion"; it is antireligious; it is a self-indulgent pastime for rich evaders of responsibility; it is ineffectual as therapy; psychoanalysis is for intellectuals; psychoanalysis is not scientific; because of the time and money required to become an analyst, the practice of psychoanalysis is restricted to a sociologic elite; because of the time and money which the patients invest, the practice of psychoanalysis is lucrative. (17), (19)

From this melange of attack and criticism, I shall address myself at this time to the issue of psychoanalysis for an elite of patients and an elite of practitioners.

At times it is difficult to ascertain whether the target of these attacks is essentially Freudian psychoanalysis, or also its revisionist modifications and expansions, or simply psychotherapy per se (excluding, of course, operant conditioning!) One also needs to disentangle the criticisms arising from those desirous of somehow extending the benefit of psychoanalysis to a wider economic and sociologic range of persons from the attacks by those who simply think no version of the method is, at best, of any use. Though I speak of attacks on the American scene, I imagine they are not unknown to our colleagues from other countries.

Having given the criticisms in headline, so to speak, I hasten to state that, though the notion of psychoanalysis for an elite has been voiced negatively, both by outsiders and by persons in the field, it has also been asserted by some of our colleagues either as a matter of fact or as a matter of pride.

Presented at the III International Forum of Psychoanalysis, Mexico City, August, 1969.

48

[[RunningHead]]

Brief Family Therapy in the Course of First Pregnancy: A Clinical Note

Max Deutscher Ph.D.

Max Deutscher

Max Deutscher, Ph.D.
390 West End Avenue
New York, N.Y. 10024

Max Deutscher  

PSYCHOANALYTIC FORMULATIONS about the psychology of pregnancy are increasingly concerned with parenthood rather than motherhood alone. This shift has united the family by bringing back the father to mother and child, and the husband to his wife—a return that enriches all who are involved and has useful conceptual and clinical applications. Earlier formulations, unduly influenced by simplistic extensions of biology into psychology, erroneously equated the biological functions of conceiving, carrying, and bearing the child, as well as nourishing him afterward, with motherhood—ignoring the fact that human loving is a social phenomenon and that the child from point of conception onwards must be humanly sponsored by both parents in a family setting if all are to prosper. It had of course been recognized that pregnancy is a high point in woman's specific functioning as a female; what was obscured is that it is also a high point in man's functioning as a male, and for both of them as family members. It is this pregnancy, which makes "parents out of spouses and a family out of a marriage, " that is the concern of this paper.

My interest in the course of pregnancy as a profound, transforming experience for the young adult was aroused in the course of my psychoanalytic work with two professional men whose wives were going through a first pregnancy. For one, there occurred an affirmation of his masculinity, capacity to care and be responsible for his wife and child, aid in differentiating himself from his historical family and in establishing his own.

Presented at the III International Forum of Psychoanalysis, Mexico City, August 1969.

[[RunningHead]]

Symbol Formation in Phobias

Edgardo Rolla M.D.

Edgardo Rolla

Edgardo H. Rolla, M.D.
Av. del Libertador 2698 120 'c'
Buenos Aires, Argentina

Edgardo Rolla  

IN THAT ORGANIZATION of personality we call "conversion hysteria, " the patient fancies that he can control persecutory objects, "the bad ones, " as if they were situated in his own body. We can observe that the patient also fantasies that he can control any anxiety over the loss or deprivation of objects with that attitude that has been called "la belle indifference." The perceptual meaningfulness of these corporal modifications, in the fantasies of these patients, is that they indicate the "locations" of those objects. These signs are not experienced as coming from phenomena occurring in the body, but as if the objects existed in space, in a "non-ego" which only seems to be localized in the body area.

In anxiety hysteria, on the other hand, the perceived signs do not originate in physical phenomena, but in objects of the external environment; that is, the "non-ego" is now in surrounding space. Yet even these are not considered, in fantasy, as signals proceeding from objects, but as signals of the individual's internal persecutory objects, which have been "situated" in space via projective identification.

In the phobias, the control of objects is accomplished, therefore, in space, which comes to be an alienated part of the personality of the individual. In place of la belle indifference of the conversion hysterias, anxiety serves the phobic person as a sign of the linkage which permits the control of a threatening world of projected objects. This is an animistic world.

In phobic ways of living bordering on psychotic disorganization, (in agoraphobia, for example) not only are the persecutory objects projected, but also "good" objects, so that what we call the "interior" of the subject has been left depopulated of the object world.

160

… to turn his hysterical misery into a current misfortune. S. FREUD 3

Psychoanalysis is a microsocial model of macrosocial contradictions and alienations. IGOR A. CARUSO 2

THERE IS AN INCREASING number of patients whose psychic conflicts have social implications. This can be ascribed to our times, marked as they are by swift changes, accompanied by the rejection of old habits and values. The central conflict with these patients seems to be a pronounced split between thought and feeling, between the past and the present. This is the historic-existential situation of the younger Brazilian generation today.

My remarks are based on my experience with a rather restricted group, mainly adults ranging in age from twenty to thirty years, students or graduates, unmarried. Broadly speaking, one may say that this psychoanalyst is a "petit bourgeois" who helps other "petit bourgeois" with their "petit-bourgeois" problems. The case discussed below is one that illustrates a certain facet of psychoanalytic practice which may not be so evident in other cases.

Virginia is a university student studying in the humanities. She sought therapy at the peak of an intense anxiety crisis, two days after having sexual intercourse with a classmate, "a kind of boy-friend."

Her father is a prosperous landowner; her mother devotes herself exclusively to household duties. The patient is derisive of the mother's submissiveness to her husband and her passive acceptance of the housewife role. The father is the object of great hostility on the part of the patient, who nevertheless concedes that she admires him greatly. The Psyche in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy11

Benjamin Wolstein Ph.D.

Benjamin Wolstein

Benjamin Wolstein, Ph.D.
2 West 67th St.
New York, N.Y. 10023

Benjamin Wolstein  

PERCEPTION OF SYMPTOMS and inquiry into their origins and functions became important very early in the history of psychoanalysis, going as far back as Breuer's and Freud's 1893–1895 Studies on Hysteria. Only recently has it been recognized, however, that becoming free of symptoms is not the same as changing psychologically. Psychoanalytic patients, today, who appear far less inhibited about adjustive sexual functions than the early id patients and far less insecure about adaptive social functions than the later ego-interpersonal patients, seem to suffer much less from unsatisfied biological needs and failed social securities than from blocked strivings for psychic freedom and personal fufillment.

It is not necessary, of course, to infer increased id satisfaction and ego-interpersonal security from decreased psychoanalytic study of them. It is possible to infer instead, for example, that id frustrations and ego-interpersonal insecurities are nothing more than symptoms that patients resolve without reporting or, perhaps more simply, that psychoanalysts no longer treat the frustrated and insecure. I tend to discount both these possible inferences and favor a third, namely that sexual satisfaction and social security no longer dominate pursuits of certain sectors of the culture at large as a result, among other things, of the wide dissemination of Freud's and Sullivan's classic findings on hysterias and obsessions beyond psychopathology into child and educational psychology, sociology and political theory, art and literature and, in important ways, even into pop culture.

[[RunningHead]]

Autism and the Phase of Transition to Therapeutic Symbiosis

Harold Searles M.D.

Harold Searles

Harold F. Searles, M.D.
5401 Westbard Avenue
Washington, D.C. 20016

Harold Searles  

THIS IS THE SECOND in a series of papers reporting my current concepts about autism, symbiosis, and individuation. I am concerned, here, not only with patients suffering from schizophrenia of whatever degree of severity, but with, for example, the subtly-present autism that emerges in the course of the neurotic patient's analysis.

In the first paper, which dealt with pathologic symbiosis and autism, I mentioned that

As the months and years of the analyst's work with the autistic patient wear on, the analyst is given to feel unneeded, incompetent, useless, callous, and, essentially, non-human in relation to his so troubled and beseeching and reproachful, but so persistently autistic, patient. It is essential that the analyst be able to endure this long period—a period in which, despite perhaps abundant data from the patient, transference-interpretations are rarely feasible—in order that the patient's transference-regression can reach the early level of ego-development at which, in the patient's infancy or very early childhood, his potentialities for a healthy mother-infant symbiosis became distorted into a defensively autistic mode of ego functioning. At that level of ego-development the infant or young child had not yet come to achieve a perceptual and experiential differentiation between himself and his mother, nor between his mother and the surrounding non-human world. When in the evolution of the transference that early level of ego-functioning becomes accessible, then it is possible for therapeutically symbiotic processes to occur between patient and analyst, and be interpretable as such. … patient and analyst … experience one another and themselves in a manner analogous to that in which a healthy mother and a healthy infant are immersed, as being far more than merely human in the adult sense, but as forming confluently a whole growth-world." 5

Meanwhile, during the autistic phase of the treatment, the analyst's attempts at transference-interpretation meet with a thoroughly defeating response. Either the patient essentially ignores them, or responds with such devastating derision and contempt as to make one feel crazy for having uttered them, or he finds them so deeply and destructively disturbing that it may require him the bulk of the hour to digest, as it were, this foreign body and expel it and restore, thus, his temporarily damaged autistic world to its state prior to this rude interruption. All this gives the analyst to feel thoroughly stupid and useless; but the patient has unconsciously thus to destroy or ignore what the analyst offers him, in order to keep repressed his own infantile need toward the analyst as a mother who is far more than a mere person—who is the whole functional world for him. To hear and accept and utilize the analyst's interpretation would mean, for the patient, the relinquishment of his only known world, in exchange for one which feels entirely unknown to him, namely, that comprised of the analyst. Hence there is an unconscious need in the patient, almost physicochemical in its primitiveness, to dissolve any bridging structure offered by the analyst in the form of transference-interpretations. The analyst senses, in general, that it is wise for him to comment only sparingly, for the relatively dispassionate emotional tone of his comments clearly has a dampening effect upon the slowly developing intensity of the schizoid patient's own emotions. It is all too easy for a calm remark from the analyst to replace a dawning aliveness in the patient with the latter's usual deadness. One can speculate, further, that a positive value can accrue, for the patient, to our not yet making any interpretative comment upon something we can clearly see in the patient: This may tend to foster integration, however inarticulate as yet, in the patient's preverbal ego.

An Administrative Behavior Pattern of Certain Obsessional Characters

Kenneth Artiss M.D.

Kenneth Artiss

Kenneth L. Artiss, M.D.
10401 Old Georgetown Road
Bethesda, Maryland 20014

Kenneth Artiss  

THE ROLE of psychiatric consultant1 to institutions and groups carries with it the unique advantage that comes to one who is privy to the confidential details of what goes on "inside" and who is at the same time a free agent whose professional or job destiny is not wrapped up in the institution itself. Under these conditions, certain behavioral patterns come into remarkably sharp focus. One of these, the effect upon the institution of placing a certain type of obsessional "Neurotic Character" in an administrative role is the subject of this report.

Most of the data are my own but, in a few instances, interested and generous colleagues have contributed case material from their files with the proviso that I keep the sources confidential. The nature of the material obviously requires this treatment and I have sought out these data because I had no other means available to fill in the gaps in my own information. I regret only that I cannot more publicly thank my colleagues for their generosity.

The subjects, twelve males, henceforth to be identified as Subject, all carried the degrees necessary to the practice of their professions—medicine, psychology, and social work. The majority were psychiatric residency trainees. Only one Subject is still practising in his specialty, all having had violent confrontations leading to their being "fired" or threatened and two having suicided under such stress.

1It would hardly be fair to say that this role has been thrust upon me, for that might imply that I have resisted it. Neither would I be correct to suggest that I have sought it, for that is not so either. Somehow, however, it has evolved and I have done a considerable amount of consulting to psychiatric and medical institutions during the past ten years.93

Sexual Contact Between Patient and Therapist11

Charles Dahlberg M.D.

Charles Dahlberg

Charles Clay Dahlberg, M.D.
516 East 87th St.
New York, N.Y. 10028

Charles Dahlberg  

MY INTEREST in this subject arose when I heard from a small number of women—not all patients of mine—that they had had sexual relations with their psychotherapists. I noted down some facts about the cases and, over a period of time, quite by accident acquired more cases; a total of nine in about twenty years of practice. I have not included in this list the gossip about the therapist whom "everybody knows sleeps with his patients, " but have confined myself to cases based on first-hand information from one of the parties involved.

The topic is such an obvious source of gossip, cartoons, and jokes that it is surprising that more has not been written about it. Parenthetically, I should note here that I have had trouble getting this paper accepted by larger organizations where I had less, but still not inconsiderable, influence. I was told it was too controversial. What a word for a profession which talked about infantile sexuality and incest in Victorian times. Although controversial was the word used, it probably was not meant in its usual sense of "disagreement." A friend offered "too hot to handle" as a more likely meaning in this instance. In any case, the object of this paper is to provoke discussion and clarification of the issues involved in a matter that has too long been kept out of the literature.

The rationalizations that therapists offer for sleeping with patients tend to be along the line of it being in the best interests of the patient.

Earlier versions were read by colleagues of the author, too numerous to mention. Of especial help were the suggestions of Joseph Barnett, Benjamin Brody, Angel Fiasché, Elaine Grimm, George Nicklin, Chaim Shatan, and William Weber.

A Survey and Reevaluation of the Concept of Penis Envy

Ruth Moulton M.D.

Ruth Moulton

Ruth Moulton, M.D.
285 Central Park West
New York, N.Y. 10024

Ruth Moulton  

PENIS ENVYsc is a concept that had made a valuable contribution to our understanding of feminine psychology. It may well be a stage through which all women pass, but it has been overemphasized and misused as a primary, basic cornerstone upon which further constructions about female development must universally rest. Penis envy is more accurately viewed as a frequent phenomenon in female sexual development which is neither primary nor universal. It plays a varying role determined by earlier predisposing factors and succeeding reinforcing ones, as well as cultural and environmental influences. Many authors have commented on the inaccuracies that necessarily accompany a phallocentric view of women. It has become increasingly clear that the male sex cannot be used as a basic standard to understand the female; each sex has innate characteristics of its own which must be evaluated in their own terms. Recent developments in embryology, physiology, endocrinology, and child development make a reevaluation of psychological sexual differences possible.

Freud himself was not satisfied with his formulations about the psychology of women. In his later years, he turned to the women in his audience and suggested that further clarification might have to come from them, since they themselves were the riddle. 8 Contributions from women analysts have differed widely and were often diametrically opposed. Marie Bonaparte 2

Based on a paper delivered at a meeting of the Association for Psychoanalytic Medicine on December 16, 1966, in New York City.

THE LITERATURE strongly supports the idea that certain communicational gestures, verbal or otherwise, on the part of one person may contribute to symptomatology in another. This theme has been elucidated in a significant body of work1 typified by Bateson et al, 2 Fleck, 6 Haley, 9 Laing and Esterson, 15 Lidz et al, 19, 20 Searles, 22 Singer and Wynne, 23 and Wynne et al. 28 In sum, the communicational stream seems to be

a sequence of contexts, both of learning and of learning to learn. … While, of course, the words that people say to each other have importance, the problem of describing the relationship between persons is not a question which can be answered by any summary of the dictionary meaning of their messages. There is a vast difference between the mechanical description "A gave B such and such information" and a description of the interchange "A answered B's question immediately." 1

The We-Self of Identical Twins

Dale Ortmeyer Ph.D.

Dale Ortmeyer

Dale H. Ortmeyer, Ph.D.
8 East 77th St.
New York, N.Y. 10021.

Dale Ortmeyer  

THE RELATEDNESS of identical twins to each other, and the intrapsychic expectancies and patterns developed therefrom, are of vital importance to the understanding of the twins' personalities and of their psychoanalytic treatment. Indeed, one reason for the persistent appearance of twins in the evolving records of man and his thought is the unexplained mystery surrounding their special unity. They have been a focus of interest, with stress on their unity, in the rituals of certain primitive tribes, 10 the myths of the Greeks, 12, 25, 23, 26 and literary works. 31, 35, 27, 3 But how can this unity be explained? They are alike in that they have an identical genetic structure and similar physical appearances. Does it also hold true that identical twins have identical personalities? Those researchers who maintain that personality is primarily genetically determined would affirm the notion of personality identity. Seen from the point of view of psychological development, the personality of twins need not be identical. There does appear to be, however, a psychological unity, a "we-self" of two personalities to some extent functioning as one.1

The psychological unity of identical twins is the focus of this paper. The author proposes that it involves a complementarity of mutually shared aspects of personality, a we-self. The emphasis is on unfortunate or non-healthful aspects of this complementarity.

SELF-SYSTEM AND WE-SELF

As Thompson 34 indicates, the concepts of self and self-system in interpersonal theory are not altogether clear. Sullivan 33 develops the idea of self-system as an enduring, relatively unchanging, learned group of attitudes sufficiently acceptable to significant others so as to minimize anxiety.

Stephen Zaslow  

THE RESOLUTION of Laura's phobia, reported below, demonstrates the usefulness of considering phase-linked ego apparatuses in evaluating regressive symptoms. It dramatically brought home to the author the need to clarify and to interpret the specific fantasies of a child in therapeutic effort. It may amplify our understanding of that common constellation of fears, the threat from below. For these reasons, it is reported here.

CASE REPORT

Laura, a bright, personable, outgoing, and to all appearances well-adjusted girl of three years and three months, suddenly refused to go to bed one night. She insisted she was "afraid I'll make a doody in my bed" and straightaway went to sit on her potty chair whenever told to go to sleep. She exhausted the usual sleep rituals of storytelling, trip to urinate, a drink of water, a good-night kiss and tuck-in. She would not stay in bed whether her parents remained in the room or not.

The parents (father, a psychologically-minded physician, mother, a former teacher) were unable to understand this precipitous regression. Despite long talk and eager listening to Laura, they got no clue they could use. She stuck to her story that she was afraid only of making a "BM" in her pants; that she really had to make now; that she had to go on the potty chair. Once on the potty, she did not defecate, nor would she consent to get off. She insisted she had to go and thus couldn't go to bed. Reassurance that she had already made that day and thus really didn't have to make again was ineffective. Review of the day's incidents was not productive.

ROBBINS EVOLVED the theory that to understand an individual dynamically, one must become aware of that person's consciousness. He defines consciousness as the sum total of an individual's attitudes, desires, needs regarding himself and others—in other words, his characterological systems of value. (4)(10)(11)(13) In his conceptualizations, conciousness represents the ever-evolving result and reflection of a person's total social and cultural experiences, and his interactions with these experiences. Also

to Robbins [as well as Masserman, Rado, and others] the term 'unconscious' referred to those aspects of the individual's value system that remained expediently unknown at a conceptual level, but which betrayed their presence in activity. (13)

A standard psychoanalytic approach might view this orientation as ahistorical and undynamic since the manipular aspect of mental disorders and the resulting secondary gain had more significance to Robbins and others than the early life experiences in the genesis of a neurosis.1 To the author, however, these premises are most historical and dynamic. A system of value does not simply come into being. It has to have a history. It is also dynamic because, on the basis of these characterological systems of value, the neurotic patient functions in his everyday life; they determine his present-day activities, experiences, and consequent suffering. Unless changed to a more constructive,

His constructive criticism of a previous draft of this article stimulated the author to more clearly think through the thesis presented in this work.2The behavioristic attitude was brought clearly into focus for the author in a recent conversation with a child therapist from a behavioristic frame of reference. When the author attempted to find some common ground between dynamic psychotherapy and the behavioristic approach, he was told, "We are not interested in what's going on in the little black box." In other words, the behaviorist does not interest himself primarily, as perhaps Robbins would have put it, with the conceptual consciousness of the patient.
